Because enterprise and personal data is usually not enough to train a foundation model, post-training is the only option, and he said the bottleneck is having models that are fully open: 'We open everything, not just the weights and the model, but the dataset as well.' He confirmed this is a funded position - NVIDIA is 'spending money to go and accumulate this dataset that we also release' - and cited a customer who took the released data and trained its own model: 'I believe it was ServiceNow who did this.' He placed the choice on a Pareto frontier of intelligence against speed, which is why a deployment needs an array of models and not one. Latency-bound workloads cannot use cloud frontier intelligence at all - his example was 'an ESPN replay at, say, Wimbledon or for the NBA' - and that is 'where edge hardware, edge AI is really important'; to run at the edge 'you have to have access to the weights', so 'The only option is to take an open-source model and train it', training a foundation model purely to run it at the edge being prohibitive. data.signal: DLSS 5 detailed at the SIGGRAPH research keynote (first glimpsed at GTC Spring earlier this year) and shipping this fall. Edward Liu, Director of Applied Deep Learning Research: DLSS 5 adds a THIRD category of AI to real-time rendering - generation - alongside reconstruction (the current DLSS suite) and function approximation (Neural Radiance Cache, Neural Materials). The renderer still builds the world and geometry is untouched; a generative model enriches appearance, conditioned on the rendered frame plus renderer internal buffers (albedos, surface normals, lighting) and motion vectors, so it runs causally, one frame in one frame out, with no shimmer or drifting. The model is distilled from giant foundation models into a much smaller one-step pixel space diffusion transformer to fit the real-time budget: a 4K frame is about 8 million pixels and at larger than 60 FPS the whole budget is less than 16 milliseconds, most of which the game itself consumes. Second scaling lever beyond rendering: scaling the model - or just better training data and loss functions - improves image fidelity at runtime with no additional runtime cost.
data.figure: 4K frame about 8 million pixels; larger than 60 FPS; less than 16 milliseconds frame budget; ships this fall

data.signal: DLSS 5 developer control surface demonstrated live by Gaff, Creative Artist: multiple DLSS 5 models (A, B, C) trained on different parameters and selectable per scene or per cut scene rather than locked per game; global structure intensity (high-frequency detail - ambient occlusion, subsurface scattering, reflections) and tone intensity (low-frequency - lighting and color); model-side auto-masking where the model understands scene semantics and can be applied to the character only; and engine-side masks, unlimited in number, each with independent intensity and tone. The demonstrated range ran from structure intensity 25%, close to the render frame, to 95%, near the maximum uplift DLSS can provide. NVIDIA said it is building more controls and working with its partners to incorporate their feedback so DLSS 5 becomes a tool for artists and art directors.
data.figure: structure intensity demonstrated from 25% to 95%

data.signal: AI surrogate models for physics simulation, presented by Neil Ashton, Researcher: an open dataset of around 2,000 aircraft simulations with more than a billion degrees of freedom generates around 200 terabytes of data; tokenized through transformer architectures developed by NVIDIA Research with research institutions, the trained model checkpoint is only around 200 megabytes - around a million times compression - and predicts an unseen geometry or boundary condition more than 10,000 times faster to within 1% or 2% accuracy, returning the flow field within a second on an RTX 6000, a relatively modest GPU, rather than hours or days, visualized with Omniverse libraries. NVIDIA supplies the stack beyond the compute: PhysicsNeMo and Earth-2 as the open source frameworks for developing these models.
data.figure: around 2,000 aircraft simulations, more than a billion degrees of freedom, around 200 terabytes -> around 200 megabyte checkpoint; more than 10,000 times faster; 1% or 2% accuracy; around a million times compression; runs on an RTX 6000

data.signal: Scale of the physics workload NVIDIA is targeting with AI (Neil Ashton): the reference coupled atmosphere-land-ocean Earth simulation ran on more than 20,000 GPUs at a resolution of one kilometer on a 50 billion cell grid and won the Gordon Bell Prize, and it is not feasible with today's technology to run a 20,000 GPU job every single day - the argument for AI surrogates. AI weather models trained on 40 years of ERA5 data autoregressively predict the next hour or day in seconds or minutes instead of hours or days, are as accurate or more accurate than traditional simulation, and weather centers around the world use these AI models in production today. StormScope, trained on satellite and observation data, predicts how storms merge and propagate orders of magnitude faster than simulation. Ashton named electromagnetics and structural simulation of cars and planes as the next domains to move.
data.figure: more than 20,000 GPUs; one kilometer resolution; 50 billion cell grid; 40 years of ERA5 data

data.signal: Cosmos world foundation model family, presented by Ming-Yu Liu, VP of Cosmos Lab: an open omnimodel on a mixture of transformers architecture with two towers - an autoregressive tower that reasons in language and a diffusion tower that generates vision, audio and action tokens - sharing multimodal attention. Action is a first-class modality encoded as geometric primitives (ego pose, effector poses, grasp and gripper), so one model covers a self-driving car, a single-arm robot, a humanoid and human egocentric video, and out of the box it supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics and policy. Cosmos 3 Nano, a 16 billion parameter model, and Cosmos 3 Super were released last month at NVIDIA GTC Taipei; Cosmos 3 Edge, a four billion parameter model built to run real-time on device - in Jetson Thor, in RTX, in DGX Spark, with no round trip to the data center - was released at this keynote. Across eight different benchmarks spanning generation, reasoning and policy, Cosmos models rank number one.
data.figure: Cosmos 3 Nano 16 billion parameters; Cosmos 3 Edge four billion parameters; number one across eight benchmarks

data.signal: Cosmos inference cost and customization (Ming-Yu Liu): Cosmos 3 Super was pre-trained with distribution matching to reduce the number of denoising steps to four, giving a 25 times speed-up for text-to-image and image-to-video generation while remaining state of the art according to Artificial Analysis. Pre-training Cosmos on the DROID dataset produced a state-of-the-art pick-and-place policy result. NVIDIA is releasing the post-training scripts it used internally to build custom models, and both the accuracy post-training and the speed post-training can be done with a DGX Station - customization does not require data-center compute.

data.signal: Cosmos platform arc and adoption (Ming-Yu Liu): Cosmos was introduced to the world in January 2025, 18 months ago, and has compounded component by component - Cosmos Predict for world generation, Cosmos Reason for world understanding, Cosmos Policy for action - all unified into a single omni-modal world model in Cosmos 3. Cosmos 3.5 has already started and will bring in multi-view and other capabilities. NVIDIA's own products are built on it: Metropolis VSS (Video Summarizing Search) for video analytics, NVIDIA Isaac for realism enhancement and variation creation in robot policy training, Cosmos Dreams, the Optane robot taxi driving policy and the GR00T humanoid policy. The platform is built with Cosmos Coalition members contributing research, data and evaluation, ships with open models, open datasets, open libraries and an open framework, and has reached millions of developers.

data.signal: Cosmos Dreams announced: a neural closed-loop simulator built on OmniDreams research, the first one for autonomous vehicles. A policy model (Optane) takes an action, Cosmos Dreams applies that action and generates what the sensors will see, photorealistic and frame by frame, at interactive speed - the car drives inside the simulator's imagination - so AV developers can verify policy accuracy before deploying the model in a real fleet and can generate scenarios difficult to craft in the real world, accelerating development velocity and saving operational cost. In the live demo an entire world was simulated from a single frame with PS5 controller input. The compute needed has collapsed across GPU generations: the demo first required 64 GB300 GPUs, then ran on 16 Vera Rubin GPUs, and now runs on a single RTX 6000 Ada Generation workstation GPU with the new Cosmos model.
data.figure: 64 GB300 GPUs -> 16 Vera Rubin GPUs -> a single RTX 6000 Ada Generation workstation GPU

data.signal: Blackwell-to-Rubin boot-drive attach step-up. Sepenzis said that with Blackwell the BlueField-3 DPU 'was an option', with an attach rate 'closer to probably 20% or 30%'. In Rubin, 'BlueField-4 is integrated. You have to buy it, so it’s 100% attached', and Silicon Motion also has boot drives in 'some of their switches, like NVLink and ethernet switches', with drive capacity rising (more units and higher ASP). The Rubin ramp will take 'probably 6-12 months.' Silicon Motion won the full BlueField-4 boot drive after the incumbent NAND maker, which had been buying Silicon Motion’s controller through a distributor, 'decided not to move forward with BlueField-4', making Silicon Motion 'the natural successor'. The customer is described as 'the world’s largest GPU maker', and the transcript names BlueField-4 and Rubin.

data.signal: Revenue reporting was recast into three end-market categories from Q4 FY2026 onward: (1) data centers, (2) communications infrastructure, (3) automotive, industrial and other. The old optical/non-optical and telecom/datacom split was retired because hyperscalers are the ultimate customer for many products previously classified as telecom. CFO Csaba Sverha: the thumb rule is 'whatever the product's getting deployed, if it's a data center or hyperscale, then it goes in the data center, everything else goes into the communication infrastructure.' A 12-quarter history under the new structure was posted; the change is presentational only with no impact on total revenue in any period.
data.figure: no specific figure

data.signal: Data center revenue was $669 million, up 68% year over year and 13% sequentially, and is now the largest category at 51% of total revenue. It covers optical and interconnect products deployed inside data centers plus an expanded view of DCI, high-performance computing and other AI infrastructure. DCI was the largest contributor to the growth, passing an annualized run rate above $1 billion; HPC also contributed substantially with solid sequential growth. Datacom was roughly flat sequentially on the reconciled basis and is guided up sequentially in Q1 FY2027.
data.figure: Data center $669M (+68% YoY, +13% QoQ), 51% of revenue; DCI annualized run rate >$1B

data.signal: Capacity roadmap raised from the ~$11.5 billion figure given last quarter to $12.5-$14 billion of revenue capacity from land and buildings already secured. Bridge from the $5.3 billion run rate exiting Q4 FY2026 ($1.32B x 4): Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion of 120,000 sq ft takes it to $5.5-$5.8B; Building 10 in Chonburi (2 million sq ft, complete by early 2027, 250,000 sq ft qualified on floor one with a similar amount on floor three qualifying this quarter) adds $3.0-$3.5B to reach $8.5-$9.3B; the newly commissioned Navanakorn building (200,000 sq ft, contributing from Q1) adds $200-$250M; the newly acquired Great America Place campus in Santa Clara (~130,000 sq ft of manufacturing, more than doubling the Silicon Valley footprint) adds $200-$250M; and two more Chonburi factories of ~1.2 million sq ft each add $1.8-$2.1B. The increase versus last quarter also reflects rising revenue per square foot, driven by revenue-dense DCI product and better space utilization. Fabrinet continues to look for more land.

data.signal: New transceiver program ramp schedule: data center transceiver business is expanding with a number of new customers and programs. The hyperscaler-direct program is among the first and starts ramping as soon as the September quarter; one merchant program begins in the December quarter; the others get off the ground in early calendar 2027. data.signal: CPO and NPO positioning: NPO (near-packaged optics) sits between pluggable modules and CPO, and Fabrinet believes it is positioned to be the leader in manufacturing and packaging NPO devices given tens of millions of pluggables built plus CPO work already underway with a handful of customers (building devices, not yet at full-scale volumes). Seamus Grady: NPO 'probably represents a more near-term opportunity than CPO from what we have seen with our customers,' and as NPO scales to 6.4T, 12.8T and beyond, manufacturing complexity and yield become critical. Revenue and margin from these programs are too early to quantify. The Raytek partnership is described as instrumental to unlocking the demand, and Raytek will add capacity in Thailand on Fabrinet's own campus so all required packaging capability sits under one roof.

data.signal: CEO Seamus Grady walked the capacity ladder to a single consolidated number: capacity right now is about $5.8 billion (the $5.3 billion Q4 exit run rate plus the Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion); Building 10 when fully available adds about $3.5 billion at the high end; Nava, the new factory in Nava Nakorn, adds about $250 million; and the newly acquired Santa Clara operation adds about another $250 million - which gets to $9.8 billion of capacity in calendar Q1, early in the March quarter, an 85% increase versus where the year ended. Beyond that, Building 11 - not yet announced - would take probably 18 months to build and add capacity for another $2.1 billion approximately, and the same for Building 12, so over the next three years Fabrinet could add another $4.2 billion on top of the $9.8 billion, taking it to approximately $14 billion of capacity. Even with all of that, Fabrinet is still looking for more land in Bangkok, in Thailand.

data.signal: Grady quantified the build-ahead economics of Building 10: it is about a 2 million sq ft factory costing about $132 million, $133 million for the building, and even if it were to sit idle the gross margin headwind is about 15 basis points, while just over five months' worth of operating profit at full run rate would pay for the whole factory. It will not sit idle - Fabrinet is already installing equipment and getting going on Floor 1 and will start to occupy Floor 3 in October. 'The downside risk is tiny and the upside opportunity is immense', with the real downside being that if the capacity is not put in place customers have to go somewhere else. Fit-out follows the customer: generic or standard equipment is paid for by Fabrinet, product-specific or unique equipment is paid for by the customer.
data.figure: idle Building 10 gross margin headwind about 15 basis points; just over five months' worth of operating profit pays for the factory; building cost about $132 million, $133 million

data.signal: CFO Csaba Sverha on funding the expansion: total CapEx for the last year was about $250 million and the company anticipates these elevated levels continue in fiscal 2027 in this $250 million range, covering the finishing of Building 10 and the fit-outs plus the Santa Clara facility that was just acquired for $76 million. Fabrinet took a small $75 million term loan signed with a Thai bank in August to finance growth in Thailand and is expanding credit lines, but is very comfortable with the balance sheet and comfortable financing growth from its own free cash flow rather than equity, because return on invested capital is close to the 40% mark. On the Q1 guide, the usual first-quarter merit salary increases add about 20, 30 basis point headwinds sequentially, which management expects to make up with efficiencies through the year.
data.figure: CapEx about $250 million last year and in the $250 million range in fiscal 2027; Santa Clara acquired for $76 million; $75 million term loan; ROIC close to the 40% mark; Q1 seasonality 20, 30 basis point headwind

data.signal: Datacom diversification status: Fabrinet is actually shipping to both hyperscale-direct and merchant transceiver manufacturers right now, and it is early days. The non-NVIDIA datacom customers are mostly initially 800 gig short reach transceivers and then moving to 1.6 in the future, with the initial foray at 800 gig. Grady reiterated Fabrinet will never become an ODM or own the IP - companies like Ciena, Cisco and Nokia would be deeply upset if it became a product company - and said Fabrinet has been picking up and winning business with some customers precisely because some competitors chose the ODM route. Management said it does not overly analyse share (customers do not always disclose it) and focuses instead on growing each opportunity to the multi-$100 million level where it can properly resource the customer. Beyond hyperscale, Fabrinet is also working with quantum compute customers that would fall into the new data center category, because moving those workloads around will need optics and not just electronics.
data.figure: no specific figure

data.signal: First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.
data.figure: typical COGS about 70%-80% material, 20% value add

data.signal: OCS ramp timing put on the clock for the first time: Fabrinet has shipped some OCS product but it is quite small today, and is working with a number of companies, one of whom it is actually shipping product to, while the others are early days and more startup-type companies. Management is looking forward to really beginning to ramp that over the next 12 to 18 months. On Coherent specifically, Grady said Coherent has a lot of its own in-house capacity at both the system level and the wafer level and does a lot of the in-house silicon itself, so he believes Coherent will continue to manufacture in-house. Fabrinet is happy to do sub-assemblies or the finished product, whatever the customer wants.
data.figure: ramp over the next 12 to 18 months

data.signal: Datacom remained supply constrained, 'particularly on the leading-edge products at 200 gig per lane, both 800 gig and 1.6'. Demand continues to outstrip supply and Fabrinet continues to ship significant volumes to its main customer but 'could ship more if we had more components'. The EML laser has been the main cause of the constraint; the customer approved a 'second source for the EML for the laser' during the quarter, which should benefit Q3 and future quarters - management says it is 'starting to see that resolution come through now'. Datacom output is almost all 200 gig per lane (1.6 terabits and 800 gig, built on the same production line); the 800G/1.6T mix is the customer's decision and not important to Fabrinet.

The $1B+ cohort is described as a lot of emerging Neoclouds and CSPs plus some enterprise customers. FY2027 revenue guided to $65-72B.
data.figure: $60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

data.signal: Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
data.figure: Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

data.signal: Supermicro disclosed approximately $39 billion of orders received in recent weeks for its advanced AI servers, including its Data Center Building Block Solutions, from more than 20 customers, which it plans to fulfill in future quarters; the company states these orders do not constitute firm commitments and are subject to cancellation and delays.
data.figure: ~$39 billion of AI server orders from more than 20 customers

data.signal: Customer concentration and mix (CFO): one large data center customer (not named) was approximately 63% of total Q2 revenue. OEM appliance and large data center revenue was $10.7 billion, approximately 84% of revenue versus 68% last quarter (up 151% YoY and 210% QoQ). By geography the U.S. was 86% of Q2 revenue (U.S. revenue up 184% YoY), Asia 9%, Europe 3% and the rest of the world 2%. Asked whether the 63% customer had been a 10% customer before, the CFO said only that Super Micro 'does most of its business with repeat customers' and has 'added a lot of new logos', and referred to the 10-K and 10-Qs. The CEO said the customer base now has 'many more large-scale customers' and is becoming more diversified, although customers sometimes pull in or push out their schedules.
data.figure: one customer approximately 63% of total revenue; OEM appliance and large data center $10.7 billion (approximately 84% of revenue); U.S. 86% of revenue

data.signal: Working capital funds the order ramp (CFO): Q2 closing inventory was $10.6 billion, up from $5.7 billion in Q1, 'as we prepared for continuing strength in Q3 shipments'. The cash conversion cycle improved from 123 days to 54 days. Operating cash use was $24 million, capex $21 million and free cash flow negative $45 million. Cash was $4.1 billion against $4.9 billion of bank and convertible note debt, for net debt of $787 million. New funding: a $2 billion secured revolving credit facility in the U.S., an approximately $1.8 billion secured Taiwan revolving debt facility closed in January, and an accounts receivable factoring facility (unused in the December quarter, used since), giving 'access to over $5 billion of additional capital'. The CFO tied the rise in receivables and inventory to having 'well in excess of $13 billion of orders' for delivery, as he had said the previous quarter.
data.figure: inventory $10.6 billion (from $5.7 billion); well in excess of $13 billion of orders; access to over $5 billion of additional capital; net debt $787 million

data.signal: Networking is now an explicit DCBBS pillar: the total solution spans CPU and GPU compute, storage, energy and a 1.6T HIGH-SPEED SWITCH plus 'upcoming optical networking', sold with the Supermicro management software suite (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM). The new 32-acre Silicon Valley DCBBS campus features an ADVANCED OPTICAL PHOTONICS NETWORKING LAB alongside datacenter-scale manufacturing, and management calls out high-speed switch and optical technology as areas of very aggressive continued investment, with the 'high bandwidth switch and the whole networking design management tool' cited as a big room to grow toward the ~20%-of-gross-profit DCBBS target. Customer networking readiness (alongside power and cooling) was one of the causes of the Q4 revenue push-out.
data.figure: 1.6T switch shipping in DCBBS; optical networking upcoming; SV photonics lab

data.signal: Transforming from a US server maker into a total data-center solution provider via DCBPS (Data Center Building Block Solutions) — complete DLC facilities, cooling units, networking, power shelves, battery backup, management software and service; DCBPS expected to contribute >25% of total profit within a few years. Data-center/cloud management software (SuperCloud Composer, managing tens of thousands of systems/racks) revenue grew from <$10M/qtr to $34M last quarter to $46M+ this quarter. Expanding capacity (Taiwan, Malaysia ramping; new ~4M sq ft Silicon Valley DCBPS campus with clean room for DLC subsystems and optical-photonics networking) toward >6,000 of the most powerful racks per month. DLC leadership = industry's fastest time-to-online.

Announced a new 32-ACRE DCBBS campus in Silicon Valley featuring an advanced optical-photonics networking lab and datacenter-scale manufacturing, bringing the U.S. footprint to nearly 4 million square feet; Taiwan, Malaysia and the NETHERLANDS facilities are also ramping strongly.

data.signal: Power and cooling readiness at the CUSTOMER site was the direct cause of the Q4 revenue shortfall - short-term customer delays in power, cooling and networking pushed revenue out of Q4 into subsequent quarters. DCBBS is the response: a turnkey stack of DLC solutions, CDU, chill door, water tower, power shelves/battery backup, 1.6T high-speed switching and networking, Supermicro Data Center Management software (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM Orchestration Manager) and full lifecycle services, plus a new PROACTIVE SERVICE model going online early next quarter where management software and field teams auto-alert and pre-stage repairs to stop compute capacity loss. DCBBS was previously guided to ~20% of gross profit and management says '20% should be not far away'. Liquid cooling penetration keeps rising - GPU and CPU platforms alike (Vera, Rubin) are liquid-cooling-ready and management expects liquid cooling to dominate the datacenter business soon.

data.signal: First full-year size for the software and services line: SVP of Corporate Development Michael Staiger said 'software and services, I think, in fiscal 2026, we just finished $538 million and growing, so it can be a substantial part of the business', and that it is higher margin. The management stack (SuperCloud Composer, Data Center Manager, Orchestration Manager) is not sold standalone - 'It's part of the solution... It'll go with our systems' - and is the control plane for racks, cooling and storage. data.signal: Management's own market-size and share math, which it had not laid out before: 'the TAM itself has been segmented out as $2 trillion-$4 trillion... if we're thinking it's $2 trillion-$4 trillion, and we're 10% of that market, and we've said this before, we're 10% now of the market itself... that gives us a $200 billion look'. data.signal: Sovereign demand is moving from indirect to direct. Staiger: 'We have more than several sovereign deployments as we speak globally. They're clearly spending. I think the early motion was enterprise spending was into the neoclouds. Sovereign spending was into the neoclouds. We were capturing it early on, but we're seeing clear evidence of them moving forward and putting factories on the floor and expanding there.' data.signal: Structural explanation of the neocloud channel: 'If you think about what's happening at the neocloud level, and you see some of these major contracts where these neoclouds were, many of them and growing, that we're serving, they're getting hyperscaler contracts. In essence, our systems at the neoclouds are serving the hyperscalers. So they need to get those systems up and running immediately.' Deployment scale cited for these operators is '100 to 1,500 rack deployments', where slow stand-up destroys economics (Staiger cited a partner's figure that 8 racks taking 30 days to become operational costs about $3 million). That is the argument for L11/L12 integrated DCBBS racks - power, cooling, CDUs, rear door heat exchangers, storage, switching and software - over shipping bare racks, and for the higher margin content that comes with it.
data.figure: 100 to 1,500 rack deployments; 8 racks taking 30 days to stand up costs about $3 million (partner figure cited by management)

data.signal: Management restated the scale trajectory in its own terms and dismissed the recurring ODM-displacement concern: 'a couple of years ago we were $1.5 billion, and now we're on our way to doing $15 billion for a year, and now we're on our way to do $15 billion for one quarter and beyond'; 'The order book, obviously, at $60 billion, underpins the guidance for the year.' On the risk that mature neoclouds switch to Taiwanese ODMs: 'That concern was around at $7 billion, at $15 billion, at $22, at $39, and it is going to exist at $68.' He also said '75% growth at these numbers is pretty significant on a year-over-year basis', and that hyperscalers doing their own silicon expands rather than shrinks the number of rack platforms Supermicro must support - fragmentation 'would be difficult to theoretically mass produce'.

data.signal: DCBBS (Data Center Building Block Solutions) economics and roadmap (CEO): DCBBS accounted for 4% of profit in the first half of fiscal 2026. DCBBS profit should contribute meaningfully in 2H FY2026 and reach 'at least double-digit contribution by end of calendar 2026'. In about a year the line grew to more than 10 key subsystems: CDU, heat exchanger, chilled doors, power shelves, battery backup, water tower, dry-towers, high-speed switching, data center management software and service. It is sold globally as a one-stop shop to large, mid-size and small data center builders to shorten time-to-deployment and time-to-online and to reduce power and water consumption.

data.signal: Industry leadership in optical networking via silicon photonics + silicon-germanium (SiGe). Launched SCALE (Silicon Photonics Co-packaged Advanced Light Engine) — the industry's first OCI-MSA-capable NPO/CPO optical-module platform, with specs exceeding the MSA (OCI MSA founders include AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI); executed tape-outs for two CPO design wins on the OCI scale-up standard. SiGe (TIAs/drivers for electrical<->optical conversion) demand strong — Vermont fab oversubscribed into 2027, margin-accretive, expanding capacity. On track to roughly DOUBLE silicon-photonics revenue in 2026 and reach a >$1B silicon-photonics run-rate exiting 2028; now designed in at 3 of the top 4 pluggable optical-transceiver companies (1.6T solutions, roadmap to 3.2T+). Partnerships at OFC: Senko (detachable fiber), Corning + EXFO (CPO ecosystem), Siltech (200G/lane receiver PICs for pluggables).

One month later GF announced SCALE (Silicon Photonics Co-packaged Advanced Light Engine), the industry's FIRST OCI-MSA-capable complete optical module platform for NPO/CPO, with specs exceeding MSA requirements (natively broadband fiber coupling minimizing insertion loss). Q1 saw tape-outs at Malta, NY for a PAIR of CPO design wins supporting the OCI standard.
data.figure: OCI MSA founders: AMD/Broadcom/NVIDIA/Meta/Microsoft/OpenAI; SCALE = first OCI-capable platform

SiGe TIAs/drivers are 'required on virtually every data center connection' with Vermont fab oversubscribed well into 2027. Company-wide design wins +50% YoY. Full-year 2026 growth for the end market was RAISED to 50-60% from a prior expectation of high-30s percent. The implied exit rate is roughly $350 million per quarter, and management reaffirmed the long-term model of 30-plus percent year-over-year growth for this end market into 2027 and beyond.
data.figure: CID ~16% of Q2 revenue, +20% QoQ, +62% YoY; FY2026 growth raised to 50-60% (from high-30s); ~$350M/quarter exit rate

data.signal: Silicon photonics revenue reported within comms infrastructure and data center is now expected to MORE THAN DOUBLE in 2026 versus the prior year. GF secured 7 new optical networking design wins in Q2 across both pluggable transceiver suppliers and major hyperscaler and networking players, and is actively engaged with 4 OF THE TOP 5 optical transceiver players. Pluggables contribute the vast majority of silicon photonics revenue today. High-volume manufacturing of 200-gig-per-lane technology is underway, 400-gig capability has already been demonstrated, and the multiyear roadmap advances module enablement to 1.6T, 3.2T and beyond. GF has more than 40 silicon photonics customers, and CEO Tim Breen said GF is on track and potentially ahead of the growth targets set for end-2028 through 2030. He also cited an expectation that 70% of data center links will be optical by 2030, calling that 'perhaps even conservative' given scale-up as well as scale-out penetration.
data.figure: Silicon photonics revenue to more than double in 2026; 7 new design wins in Q2; engaged with 4 of top 5 transceiver players; >40 SiPho customers; 200G/lane in HVM, 400G/lane demonstrated

data.signal: SCALE, described as the industry's first OCI MSA compatible solution for near and co-packaged optics, has 7 ACTIVE ENGAGEMENTS with leading companies. GF taped out a SCALE-related design win in Q2 and expects to tape out another in Q3. Management reiterated a consistent timeline: the NPO ramp BEGINS IN 2027 and the CPO ramp BEGINS IN 2028. Because near and co-packaged optics are built on a common photonic IC - an EIC bonded to a PIC with a micro-optic and a fiber-attached unit - and differ mainly in that NPO is bonded to the board while CPO sits within the package (plus SerDes architecture differences), GF expects to benefit regardless of which form factor customers adopt. Many customers are pursuing both, with NPO ramping sooner. Breen attributed the sudden industry interest in NPO to SerDes synergies that make the system transition smaller than a jump straight to full CPO, and expects pluggables, NPO and CPO all to coexist in the data center.
data.figure: 7 active SCALE engagements; 1 SCALE tape-out in Q2 and another expected in Q3; NPO ramp begins 2027, CPO ramp begins 2028

data.signal: GF entered a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a $300 MILLION award to accelerate next-generation silicon photonics technologies in the U.S. The funding supports three components: continued PIC-level innovation and improved modulator technology to reach 400-gig per lane and beyond; NEW MATERIALS to be introduced into the system - management named barium titanate, thin-film lithium niobate and indium phosphide; and packaging capability and capacity for the integrated optical engines needed for near and co-packaged optics, building directly on the SCALE platform. Management said the endorsement came from the world's top XPU providers, hyperscalers, AI connectivity leaders and ecosystem partners.
data.figure: $300M U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for next-generation silicon photonics

data.signal: Silicon germanium is OVERSUBSCRIBED THROUGHOUT 2027 and, notably, GF's SiGe business is LARGER THAN ITS SILICON PHOTONICS BUSINESS TODAY. GF secured multiple new SiGe TIA and driver design wins across networking customers in the quarter. The growth has two compounding drivers: the shift to optical networking itself, and the fact that what could previously be done in CMOS at 50-gig and 100-gig per lane cannot be done at 200-gig and definitely not at 400-gig per lane, forcing transimpedance amplifiers and increasingly the drivers out into high-performance analog processes like SiGe. High-performance analog also appears in near and co-packaged optics depending on architecture. GF is expanding SiGe capacity at Burlington, Vermont and qualifying 300-millimeter SiGe in Singapore for additional capacity, better economics and higher fT/fMAX performance. The SiGe lineage traces to IBM Microelectronics, which invented SiGe and is part of GF today.
data.figure: SiGe oversubscribed throughout 2027; SiGe business larger than silicon photonics today; Vermont capacity expanding, 300mm SiGe qualifying in Singapore

data.signal: Capacity strategy is a structural advantage: GF is adding capacity WITHIN ITS EXISTING FAB FOOTPRINT rather than building new fabs, which management contrasted with competitors on longer lead times. Breen said GF 'could 10x our photonics capacity within our current 4 walls' globally on its long-term plan. Q2 utilization was in the high 80s, leaving about 10 points of headroom to grow into with installed capacity. Confidence in bringing capacity online plus factory productivity improvements was cited as a direct contributor to raising the full-year CID outlook. On competition in silicon photonics, Breen said customers are coming to GF saying they do not have enough capacity secured and want more, partly to mitigate geopolitical risk, and he sees no customer-concentration concern given 40-plus customers.
data.figure: Photonics capacity expandable ~10x within existing fabs; Q2 utilization high-80s with ~10 points of headroom

data.signal: GF implemented PRICING INCREASES in partnership with customers across several technology corridors during Q2, following what management called constructive conversations. The adjustments will be reflected in revenue COMMENCING IN 2027, with magnitude varying by end market and technology based on differentiated value, supply/demand dynamics and inflationary absorption. GF will continue assessing 2027 pricing through the second half of 2026.
data.figure: Price increases agreed across several technology corridors, revenue impact commencing 2027

data.signal: GF launched Quantum Technology Solutions in May 2026, a dedicated team aimed at taking the quantum industry from prototypes to high-volume production. The strategy is qubit-agnostic across superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological and spin modalities, using the FDX platform as a cryogenic CMOS foundation and extending advanced packaging into the cryogenic regime for 3D heterogeneous integration. GF is working with 8 of the world's leading quantum computing players including PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Quantum Motion plus endorsements from the quantum arms of large hyperscalers, and has already begun 4 new customer-specific engagements in the three months since launch. The effort is anchored by an expected $375 MILLION grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Over the next 1 to 3 years quantum revenue comes largely through engineering engagements booked in technology services, with manufacturing-services revenue ramping toward the end of the decade. Several quantum players are working on the photonics side of their solutions, which maps directly onto GF's silicon photonics roadmap.
data.figure: $375M expected U.S. Department of Commerce quantum grant; 8 leading quantum players engaged; 4 new customer engagements in 3 months

data.signal: IP, software and custom silicon: GF completed the acquisition of the Synopsys ARC processor IP Solutions business in June, adding CPU, DSP, NPU and RISC-V technologies, a software development toolkit and application-specific processor design capability - over 150 patents, 300 existing customers and 400 R&D engineers. Combined with MIPS, this lets GF engage customers earlier in the design cycle for edge AI and on-device inference in automotive, industrial and robotics. Full-year 2026 technology services contribution from MIPS plus ARC was RAISED to $100-120 million from a prior $60-100 million, skewed roughly one third Q3 and two thirds Q4, and technology services revenue is now expected toward the high end of the 10-12% of total revenue range with gross margin significantly above corporate targets. Design wins in the quarter included 3 strategic chiplet wins with Lockheed Martin on FinFET and FDX, an expanded FinFET win with Microchip, a first-ever PMIC design win with MediaTek on the BCD platform, an ADAS radar tape-out for Bosch on FDX, and a new microLED display backplane win for augmented reality wearables at a leading hyperscaler.
data.figure: Technology services contribution raised to $100M-$120M for 2026 (from $60M-$100M); ARC adds 150 patents, 300 customers, 400 R&D engineers

data.signal: End-market split and the memory-shortage read-across: smart mobile devices were ~36% of Q2 revenue, up 15% sequentially but down 6% year over year, and are now expected to DECLINE BY A LOW-TEENS PERCENTAGE in 2026 because 2026 handset forecasts have been cut meaningfully on continued memory pricing and associated shortages. Automotive was ~19% of revenue, down 13% sequentially and 10% year over year on customer-led shipment timing, but full-year low-double-digit growth is still expected weighted to Q4. Home and industrial IoT was ~19% of revenue, up 30% sequentially and 10% year over year - its fastest year-over-year growth since 2022 - and the full-year outlook was raised to 10-15% growth from mid-single digits, partly because mobile customers reallocated demand into IoT connectivity applications. data.signal: VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.

data.signal: Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.

data.signal: WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.

data.signal: CALL — OPEN CPO STANCE AND THE SCALE-UP VIEW: scale-up philosophy = 'COPPER IF YOU CAN, OPTICS IF YOU MUST.' Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' Scale-up positioning: 'we live in an NVIDIA world' — where NVIDIA supplies the full NVLink vertical stack there is little Arista participation (Arista wins scale-out/across), but for NON-NVIDIA accelerators (AMD MI series, Google TPUs — 'increasingly a FORMIDABLE training processor', in-house XPUs, inference chips) Arista works BOTH scale-up and scale-out, including CUSTOM RACKS tuned to customers' engines; 'feels like InfiniBand 2-3 years ago... it will take time to move from proprietary NVLink to alternatives, even if Ethernet's really good — I expect us to do much better there.' 1.6T cadence (history repeats 800G's trials-2023/24 -> ramp-2025/26): TRIALS H2 2026 with single-digit VERY LARGE customers; REAL PRODUCTION 2027 (liquid-cooling infrastructure required). EOS innovations for AI fabrics: SSU hitless upgrades, MRC packet-spray/reassembly (kills hash-collision slowdowns), SRv6 explicit-path load balancing with real-time congestion signals — one binary from scale-out to scale-across.
data.figure: Open CPO (socketed/NPO) trials 2027; majority stays pluggable+copper, some CPO 2028-29; non-NVIDIA scale-up = the opening (InfiniBand analogy); 1.6T production 2027

The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. data.signal: GaN roadmap: 'This year, we are preparing to sample more than 30 new GaN devices spanning 40 to 1,200 volts, including both discrete devices and integrated driver plus GaN solutions', from low-voltage parts near the XPU to 1,200-volt parts for automotive and industrial. data.signal: Dragonfly G5 strategy clarified: management does NOT expect a G3-to-G5 transition. data.signal: A new growth leg is forming in power semiconductors from data center power. Onto's earlier power-semi run was driven not by capacity expansion but by customers using Onto's inspection and metrology to drive yield improvement, with yields in the 60%-70% range rather than the 90s. The EV recovery has not really happened yet, but those same customers are now telling Onto they see demand from data centers driving adoption of power semiconductors and that Onto needs to prepare. Management is not seeing the actual orders yet and has no good clarity on timing, but said 2027 into 2028 is what the customers are thinking about; because the process control is already inserted in their process, Onto should benefit as they expand. Data center power is relatively small for Onto today and would be captured under specialty devices.

data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
data.signal: CFO Brian Roberts on the margin path and supply: 2026 margin gains have come from operational productivity and the move of manufacturing from the U.S. to the international extended factories - a year ago Onto was shipping its first tools from those factories and in Q2 it shipped about 70% of its tools from them. To date Onto has driven 250 basis points of gross margin and doubled that at the operating margin line. Into 2027, the accretive Dragonfly G5 and Atlas G6 add ASP lift which, alongside productivity, drives toward 'a margin that starts with a six'. The two major 2026 headwinds were memory cost and freight/fuel shortage, partly offset by being in region, and Onto is having pricing conversations with customers about the existing product portfolio for the 2027 pricing/budgeting season. On supply, the extended-factory move gave Onto partner capacity and new clean rooms without heavy CapEx; the supply chain is not perfect but Onto is using customer visibility to get ahead of bottlenecks, is carrying a higher inventory balance, is not missing customer dates and its lead times have not grown too much.

data.signal: Growth split disclosed: this year the biggest growth was in packaging at 80% growth while advanced nodes was about 35% growth, and for next year management expects not those numbers but similar dynamics, with advanced packaging still probably growing stronger than advanced nodes and both growing fairly well. Within advanced packaging the memory (HBM) versus 2.5D logic mix is fairly well split, generally around the 50/50 mark or 60/40 depending on the quarter, because logic requires the memory around it so the whole packaging requirement grows across both. data.signal: First sizing of the panel-level packaging opportunity: Plisinski said Onto has publicly put the market at around a $1 billion SAM (competitors have said even more), covering process control - inspection as well as lithography - and that while Onto will not get 100% of it against competitors, '$200 million, $300 million' would be a reasonable expectation over the next few years. The accelerant is that constraints in AI packaging and heterogeneous integration are pushing customers to panel as an alternative: as die and therefore packages get bigger the economies of scale at the wafer level stop working - at 310 by 310 they get better, but that is still much smaller than 600 by 600 or 510 by 515 - so customers are moving capacity to companies with a proven process that can ramp right now. Adoption is still early and management expects it to continue over the next several years. The enterprise-server driver (advanced IC substrates, where Intel and AMD were constrained during COVID) is also working its way back, addressed by the JetStep X500 and Firefly.
data.figure: around a $1 billion SAM; Onto share expectation $200 million, $300 million over the next few years

data.signal: Next-generation inspection: Onto is supporting 4 separate customer evaluations of its next-generation inspection systems (the G5, which the analyst described as Onto's 'new high-resolution Dragonfly platform') at customers' facilities. Preliminary feedback is positive, citing significant improvement in optical performance and higher throughput. The qualifications target 2.5D packaging and high-bandwidth memory, including next-generation hybrid bonding, where current-generation tools are already used for process control and R&D. The timeline is unchanged: 'accelerated evaluations to end in the Q1, Q2, the first half of the year with hopefully starting to catch ramps in the second half of the year.' 3D metrology is becoming more crucial for die stacking and fan-out, and the 3Di metrology pipeline is expanding beyond HBM. Semilab's surface charge metrology, which addresses residual charge on die in large-format heterogeneous packaging, received its first orders.
data.figure: 4 separate customer evaluations of next-generation inspection systems; evaluations to end in the first half of the year

data.signal: Panel-level packaging: Onto won orders in the quarter for JetStep and 8 Firefly systems to support 'an exciting new large panel packaging facility'. The orders are 'the first of several potential phases of expansion', and the panel customer serves AI applications. Multiple advanced-packaging customers placed further 3Di purchase orders, including an OEM that needs precise metrology for new panel-level process development. Customers are adopting Firefly process control in glass and panel fan-out, feeding metrology into the stepper for shot-by-shot adjustments, and JetStep prints large packages without stitching. In lithography, after a period of heavy industry overcapacity, customers are 'beginning to resume orders'. Onto expects this to increase into 2027, and the data suggests 2027 'will be in supply-demand where there's just not enough supply to meet the demand'. CEO: end customers such as 'the AMDs, et cetera, are looking for alternatives' to traditional advanced packaging so they can scale.

data.source: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
data.signal: Plisinski confirmed the Rigaku transaction has closed ('First it's closed, so that's done deal') and declined to discuss further steps. He said the partnership is strategic not because OCD is running out of steam - Onto believes it can keep pushing OCD for the foreseeable future - but because as the world moves to more 3D transistors and 3D stacking of die or wafers there are elements between layers that optical cannot solve, where X-ray can see through. Onto has already started with two different customers, went up against the leading player in X-ray and beat them at both customers, on the strength of Onto's AI Diffract modelling engine combined with Rigaku's sensor/X-ray capability. The next step is hybrid metrology - the speed of optical combined with the precision of slower X-ray - made simpler because AI Diffract already aggregates and models the data streams together.

data.signal: Commercial partnership with AMD for up to 2.5 GW of data center capacity. The initial agreement represents more than $14 billion of base contracted revenue across 15-year agreements with 2.5% annual escalators, with Core Scientific delivering 530 MW across five sites: approximately 380 MW directly to AMD under a triple-net lease across Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee, and the remaining approximately 150 MW across Auburn and Dalton supporting an unnamed neocloud under a modified gross lease for which AMD provides full credit support for the full 15-year term. The credit support carries no equity step-in rights, protecting Core Scientific's equity in the projects. Core Scientific issued AMD a warrant struck at current market levels, vesting subject to certain commercial conditions. The platform is an integrated colocation platform engineered to support AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with a close-coupled design framework aligned to AMD's GPU and CPU technology roadmap. Pecos is the lead site with initial megawatt delivery in the first half of 2027; about half the contract delivers in 2027 and half in 2028. The build requires approximately $6 billion of capital at $11 million-$12 million per megawatt, to be financed through project-level bonds. AMD additionally holds an exclusive reservation right on as much as two additional gigawatts at Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee.

data.signal: NAND/DRAM scarcity is the defining constraint. CEO Wallace Kou: the AI super cycle has driven substantial HBM, DRAM, NAND and HDD price increases and 'mounting substrate and supply pressure,' and he expects the scarcity to persist 'likely until 2028 when new fabs come online.' DRAM and NAND now account for almost 56% of total BOM cost on a low-end smartphone, forcing OEMs to trim specifications; smartphone units are still expected down 10-15% in 2026. NAND makers are redirecting focus and CapEx to DRAM and HBM, deemphasising eMMC/UFS and exiting automotive - which hands share to Silicon Motion's module-maker customers and gives it stronger pricing power. Long-standing relationships let Silicon Motion secure NAND from multiple suppliers through the shortage, which management calls a significant and enduring differentiator.

data.signal: Ferri for Automotive and Enterprise Boot Drive solutions MORE THAN DOUBLED sequentially and now represent nearly 30% of total revenue, up from 4% a year ago. These are controller-plus-NAND solutions, so ASPs are much higher than controller-only (and higher than MonTitan). The DRAM-less boot drive is the crown jewel: conventional DRAM-based boot drives for server CPUs stay with the NAND makers, but DPUs, TPUs, NPUs and switches favour DRAM-less designs for cost, security and performance - and NAND makers have no DRAM-less PCIe SSD controllers and little incentive to build them for a market where densities are only 256GB-512GB. A server rack can carry more than 30 or 40 boot drives, and per-drive capacity should rise. Management sees little competition from either NAND makers or module makers, and said Ferri plus Boot Drive reaching roughly one third of revenue in 2027 is 'certainly a possibility' given current backlog and pipeline.

data.signal: 2025 revenue mix: industrial (which includes technology) was 67% of volume; technology, dominated by data center work, was 45% of revenue, up from 33% the prior year, and is the largest driver of pipeline and backlog; institutional 21%; construction 86% of revenue (new buildings 63%, existing buildings 23%); modular 18% of revenue; service revenue grew 12% to a record $1,200,000,000 and is now 14% of revenue. The CEO said advanced technology is 'overwhelmingly data center' and that good partners make it worth dedicating the overwhelming majority of Comfort's resources to that vertical; Texas (a combination of modular and stick build, where Comfort has the largest electrical contractor) is 'really probably unique in the country with the amount of build.'

data.signal: Modular capacity is currently around 3,000,000 square feet and is expected to reach approximately 4,000,000 square feet by the end of 2026, weighted to the first half; the single biggest space procurement closes in February and capacity comes online gradually over the year (final assembly space can be productive very quickly). The CFO said the expansion is 'primarily us taking steps to meet more of the demand from our two largest customers. They would buy more if they could' - the new floor space is planned for 'those two large hyperscaler customers'; a few other modular customers have been added, 'but none of them are at scale.'

data.signal: 2025 CapEx was $155,000,000, just over 1.7% of revenues (modular capacity expansion and service vehicles). For 2026 the CFO called 1.7% a baseline rate, with building purchases on top - a $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 building moves the meter a couple tenths of a percent; one very large building purchase happens in the first quarter and another very big one, probably in North Carolina, is being evaluated for lease or purchase. Comfort prefers buying these buildings because of the robotics and automation it installs: 'you really do not want to drop $30,000,000 into a $60,000,000 building you do not own.'

data.signal: Asked about possible changes to cooling requirements for next-generation chips, the CFO said the impact on Comfort is 'not at all': 'the new chip stuff—they said, okay, we can use 45-degree water. Still needs pipe. Still needs water.' He added that 45-degree water is not naturally occurring for 99% of the year in 99% of places, and that as long as servers run on electricity they produce heat, so customers will keep needing electricians and pipe fitters; the CEO said the change is 'Far more impactful for the OEMs than for us.'
data.figure: 45-degree water (next-generation chip cooling requirement cited by management)

data.signal: Construction capacity is scarce: the CFO said 'Not everybody who wants a building gets one,' and some Q4 bookings were customers trying to sign Comfort up for their projects as soon as possible. Labor is where Comfort takes all of its risk (there are no four-year price locks for labor); Comfort hires with an all-of-the-above approach plus its in-house traveling contract craft professionals (Kodiak and Pivot), has over 22,000 employees and says 'we have a lot of work to chase.' Scarcity lets it demand to be rewarded for risk and scarce resources; highly specified equipment is never quoted without a supplier quote, and customers release Comfort to buy equipment very early, sometimes before the work enters backlog. The CEO said the company stays disciplined: 'The work we have, we can handle.'
data.figure: over 22,000 employees

data.signal: Initial 2026 outlook: management is optimistic that gross profit margins will continue in the strong ranges of the last several quarters, with the usual seasonally lower first quarter (January ice storms shut jobs at some of its biggest operations for multiple days), and estimates a 2026 tax rate of around 23%; SG&A (Q4 $248,000,000, 9.4% of revenue vs 11.1%) should grow more slowly than revenue. The analyst's question cites a 2026 same-store revenue growth expectation of mid to high teens, and the reply (printed inside the analyst's turn in this transcript) repeats 'mid to high teens,' says growth should be consistent through the year and that steeper second-half comparables, not first-half weighting, drive the pattern.

data.signal: 2025 operating cash flow was $1,200,000,000 and full-year free cash flow was a record $1,000,000,000. data.signal: Biomarker-driven patient identification kept scaling in neuroscience and oncology. data.signal: Genetic-medicine capability advanced on both the science and the manufacturing side. He added that the early uptake of oral GLP-1s has been encouraging and is expanding the market of people taking incretin therapy, while injectable incretins continue to be an important growth driver and account for three out of four new patient starts.

Ilya Yuffa put the figure at about 35% more Americans able to access obesity therapy, said Lilly is working closely with CMS on prior authorization criteria and stakeholder education, and said LillyDirect has been enabled to fulfill on the Bridge process.

Ilya Yuffa said that in the last week of July Lilly is almost doubling the volume it had just a month ago, and that around one out of four new starts are on Foundayo. The prescriber base grew from the 8,000 cited on the prior earnings call to 36,000, with sampling covering the first 30 days of the first dose across the prescriber base and full supply to enable it. Marketing, selling and administrative expenses increased 25% as Lilly invested in promotional activities to support current and planned product launches.

Lilly launched in the UAE in early May, received approval in Saudi Arabia for obesity and in Mexico for obesity and Type 2 diabetes, and has the product under regulatory review in more than 40 additional markets with a global rollout in all major markets expected in 2027. Patrik Jonsson said most patients are naive to incretin treatment, that Lilly's combined incretin share held steady even with a second oral entering the UAE market, and that Lilly is extremely well-positioned in terms of supply with no gating of launches either.

data.signal: In Immunology, Ebglyss (lebrikizumab) worldwide sales more than doubled compared to Q2 2025, and in the U.S. it continued to gain share of new prescriptions, increasing by approximately 4 percentage points in the specialty dermatology market since last year. With partner Almirall, Lilly is exploring dosing once every 12 weeks with data expected in 2027, and it submitted for a pediatric atopic dermatitis indication in the U.S. based on positive phase III results in children 6 months to 18 years old in the ADorable trial program.

Dan Skovronsky said phase III BRUIN CLL-322, which added pirtobrutinib to a time-limited venetoclax and rituximab regimen in previously treated CLL, reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 45% in the overall study population and by 68% in patients whose disease progressed after one prior covalent BTK inhibitor. He called these the first results to outperform a venetoclax-containing control arm in a CLL phase III trial, with potential to establish a new standard of care, and said the data have been submitted to global regulatory authorities.

data.signal: INLURIYO continued strong uptake in the metastatic breast cancer oral SERD market: Lucas Montarce said that after only two full quarters INLURIYO is the U.S. leader in new prescriptions, with more than 50% share. Jake Van Naarden laid out the post-Verzenio breast cancer strategy, saying the three most important targets are the estrogen receptor, CDK4/6 and PI3 kinase alpha, that Lilly believes it has the best medicine for every one of them, and that it plans to combine them. Lilly is on the precipice of beginning the phase III program for tersolisib, its PI3 kinase inhibitor, initially combined with existing endocrine therapies and investigators' choice of CDK4/6 (a large part of which he expects to be Verzenio), and over time envisions combining it with INLURIYO for an all-oral regimen.

data.signal: Retatrutide's efficacy profile is opening indications beyond obesity. Dan Skovronsky said TRIUMPH-1 showed weight loss approaching bariatric surgery levels at the highest doses and clinically meaningful efficacy at low doses with only one titration step, and that in patients with diabetes and obesity retatrutide delivered a magnitude of weight loss not previously seen with incretin therapy. Ken Custer said TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1 showed knee osteoarthritis pain reduced by unprecedented amounts, 75%, that a MASH or MASLD study is ongoing where the glucagon mechanism of action may offer unique opportunities, that a chronic lower back pain study will read out sometime next year, and that Lilly is evaluating several additional indication opportunities internally.

data.signal: Dave Ricks gave the status of the retatrutide filing pathway. Lilly's position is that retatrutide is a biologic application, both in terms of the amino acid count rule and as analogous to a protein. There was a mixed decision in the first court decision and the matter is active litigation; Lilly hopes to come to a conclusion with the FDA to support a BLA application. Lilly has announced it has all the clinical data it needs to submit but still needs to gather a little more on the CMC side, and is in communication with the agency. He added that Lilly has a pretty large lead over any competitors with a triple-acting medicine.

data.signal: Lilly completed its U.S. submission of orforglipron in Type 2 diabetes, supported by the ACHIEVE phase III program, and presented detailed results from ACHIEVE-2, ACHIEVE-3 and ACHIEVE-5 at the American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions in June. Dan Skovronsky said ACHIEVE-3 was the first head-to-head comparison of two oral GLP-1s and that orforglipron delivered superior glycemic control and weight reduction against 7 mg and 14 mg oral semaglutide in patients with Type 2 diabetes, positioning it as a potential foundational daily oral treatment.

data.signal: On the shape of the second half, Lucas Montarce said Lilly is upgrading the guide by $2.5 billion for the full-year and walked through the ins and outs. The 2025 base period contains the bolus of MOUNJARO launches in all U.S. markets and new countries in the second half, which will not repeat, so future growth is driven more by penetration in the ex-U.S. market. The guide also factors in the usual Europe Q3 vacation seasonality and U.S. Type 2 diabetes seasonality in the fourth quarter. Measured in dollars rather than percentage growth, he said Lilly expects to continue to drive significant growth in the second part of the year.

data.signal: Patrik Jonsson gave the ex-U.S. competitive read. MOUNJARO continues to perform very strongly more or less everywhere and has taken a market leadership position across many different markets; in China it obtained category leadership on the NRDL already after 16 months, with significant growth also in Korea, the U.K., Mexico and Germany, and market share in many markets very similar to the level of the U.S. or even above. He said the generic companies have had significant supply constraints, something Lilly needs to monitor very closely, and that tirzepatide's superiority data is a strong first line of defense.

data.signal: Data-center architecture and future designs (CEO Dave Regnery, answering analyst questions on recent comments from a data-center partner about chillers and liquid cooling): 'we're working very closely with many influencers in the data center vertical. So think of hyperscalers, think of chip manufacturers, like Nvidia and others. We're helping them design data centers of the future. Or you may have heard them referred to as reference design data centers' - data centers to be built 'maybe two to four years out'. 'I have not seen a reference design or data center of the future that does not include chillers, just to be very clear', with 'a lot of innovation around the thermal management system, specifically around the chiller' in Trane's pipeline. Future data-center farms will build in free cooling: fans keep running through the free-cooling cycle while the compressor side runs less often; because chillers are sized to the thermal load, 'you're still gonna have the same number'. Asked whether HVAC's share of data-center spend is higher or lower two to four years out: 'I'm gonna err on the side of saying it's probably about the same', while 'the amount of power that is being consumed by the thermal management system may be less', letting operators redirect power to computing.
data.figure: no specific figure

data.signal: Data-center service economics (CEO Dave Regnery): 'hyperscalers or colos, they want the OEM to be doing the service work', and with very large data-center fields Trane is putting more dedicated resources on a single site; service attachment is far higher than a decade ago - 'I'd be hard-pressed to think where we've done a major chiller farm where we haven't had the service agreements.' The service tail on an applied thermal-management system is thought of at 'the eight to 10'; 'In data centers, look, to be honest with you, it's probably gonna be a bit lower', because compressor run-time may fall and more efficient chillers could be swapped out earlier to divert power to compute - still being modeled. Response time, uptime and connected solutions stay the same, 'So we'll still have a big robust service business.' Services are about one-third of enterprise revenue with a low-teens CAGR since 2020.
data.figure: applied thermal-management service tail at the eight to 10 (data centers probably a bit lower); services about one-third of enterprise revenue

data.signal: Capacity for the applied ramp (CEO Dave Regnery / CFO Chris Kuehn): 'our chiller capacity over the last, you know, two or three years is up over four x', through new builds, lean work and new lines. Management also works with supply-chain partners on their capacity because 'their ability could hinder us if we're not careful' - 'we're in good shape there'. Trane commissions its applied systems with its own field force of over 7,500 technicians globally. Asked about capex, the CFO confirmed the analyst's capex-to-revenue range for the last few years ('You're right, Jeff') and said 'it's been able to support all the capacity expansions we needed to do', and that 'we brought in businesses on air handling or industrial process cooling capacity for data centers' via M&A, which adds capacity inside Trane's four walls. On lead times: no dramatic change for at least twelve months, Trane is 'very competitive on our lead times' and has introduced quick ship programs.
data.figure: chiller capacity up over four x (last two or three years); over 7,500 technicians

data.signal: Stellar Energy acquisition and capital deployment (CFO Chris Kuehn / CEO Dave Regnery): the largest acquisition, announced in December, is Stellar Energy, 'a leading provider of turnkey data center cooling solutions' with modular design-and-build capability for prefabricated cooling systems 'that ease supply chain and labor constraints and enable rapid scalable deployment'; expected to close in the first quarter with modest EPS accretion in 2026 after year-one acquisition and integration costs. Stellar builds modular chiller plants that 'get assembled on a job site like Legos', moving skilled labor and testing back to the factory; it is 'predominantly right now in the data center vertical', with 'some overlap' in customers and 'a lot of opportunities for this modular concept in core verticals as well'. In 2025 Trane deployed or committed approximately $3.2 billion (about $840 million dividends, $720 million M&A, roughly $1.5 billion share repurchases); for 2026 it expects to deploy between $2.8 billion and $3.3 billion, with $4.7 billion remaining under the repurchase authorization.

data.signal: Breadth and geography of demand (CEO Dave Regnery): 'we had 12 of 14 that were positive' among the Americas verticals tracked (life science was not), with data centers very strong alongside retail and office; the data-center vertical is 'almost all' new construction while core verticals skew to retrofit. data.signal: Total gross margin was 66% versus 59% a year earlier, with software gross margin of 89% versus 81% and services gross margin of 33% versus 25%. Management attributed the software margin increase to higher development and discovery software revenue and lower software-related costs, largely reduced amortization following the impairment charge in the third quarter of fiscal 2025.
data.figure: total gross margin 66% vs 59%; software 89% vs 81%; services 33% vs 25%

data.signal: The company ended the quarter with 297 commercial clients, average revenue per client of $124,000 and a 91% renewal rate for the quarter; on a trailing-twelve-month basis average revenue per client was $148,000 and the renewal rate was 87%. Logo retention has been 100% for top 20 pharma and 90% for pharma generating over $1 billion in global revenue, with churn concentrated in smaller commercial pharma and pre-commercial biotech. The top 25 customers represent about 46% of software revenue with 100% logo retention and over 90% gross revenue retention.
data.figure: 297 commercial clients; ARPU $124,000; renewal 91% (TTM ARPU $148,000, renewal 87%); top 25 customers ~46% of software revenue

data.signal: Total services projects worked on during the quarter were 199 and ending backlog increased 18% to $24 million from $20.4 million last year. Development services, which include biosimulation services, increased 12% for the quarter at 77% of services revenue, while commercialization MedComm services declined 1% for the quarter but grew 66% on a trailing-twelve-month basis.
data.figure: backlog $24M (+18%) from $20.4M; 199 services projects; development services +12% (77% of services revenue)

data.signal: Simulations Plus announced strategic collaboration programs with three large pharmaceutical companies to advance AI workflows across the drug development life cycle, using GastroPlus, MonolixSuite, ADMET Predictor and PKpluS. Participating companies integrate internally developed AI agents directly into model-informed drug development workflows for natural language interaction, automated data processing and coordination of simulations across multiple modeling engines. Management said there has already been a financial component to at least one relationship, that long-term commercial terms are still under discussion, and that AI is expected to become a contributor in fiscal year 2027 rather than fiscal 2026.
data.figure: 3 large-pharma AI collaboration programs across 4 platforms; AI monetization expected to contribute from fiscal 2027

data.signal: Fiscal 2026 guidance was left relatively unchanged at total revenue of $79 million-$82 million, year-over-year growth of 0%-4%, software mix of 57%-62% and adjusted EBITDA margin of 26%-30%, with adjusted diluted EPS now $0.75-$0.85 reflecting an effective tax rate raised to 23%-25% from a previous 12%-14%. Third-quarter guidance is revenue of $20 million-$22 million, adjusted EBITDA margin of 27%-33% and adjusted diluted EPS of $0.20-$0.27. The company ended the quarter with $41.8 million in cash and short-term investments and no debt.
data.figure: FY2026 revenue $79M-$82M (0%-4% growth); adjusted EBITDA margin 26%-30%; adjusted EPS $0.75-$0.85; Q3 revenue $20M-$22M; cash $41.8M, no debt

data.signal: Drug-design efficiency: candidates are being advanced with roughly 330 synthesized compounds over about 1.5 years versus an industry benchmark of roughly 2,500 compounds over four years. REC-7735 was designed in 10 months using 242 compounds across 13 cycles and is nearly 130x selective over wild type.
data.figure: ~330 compounds / 1.5 years vs ~2,500 / 4 years; REC-7735: 242 compounds, 13 cycles, 10 months

data.signal: Agentic workflows are in production across biology, chemistry and clinical development. The chemistry design agent compresses structural-analysis cycles from roughly four hours to about 30 minutes, while clinical workflows are contributing to approximately 1.3x-1.6x better enrollment versus historical benchmarks. Nesso-1 delivers stated Boltz-2-level accuracy with 10x-20x faster inference.
data.figure: 4 hours -> ~30 minutes; enrollment +1.3x-1.6x; inference 10x-20x faster
